chunks: Ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Hishām ibn Sālim, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
Some of the family of Zurārah asked him about a man who cut out the tongue of a mute man. He said, and so he said:

If his mother gave birth to him while he was mute, then one-third of the diyah is due upon him. And if his tongue was taken away by pain or an affliction after he had been speaking, then upon the one who cut out his tongue is one-third of the diyah of his tongue.
He said: “And likewise is the judgment concerning the two eyes and the limbs.” He said: “And thus we found it in the Book of ʿAlī عليه السلام.”

key_terms.آفَةٌ: an affliction or impairment that damages bodily ability
key_terms.أَخْرَسَ: a mute person, one unable to speak
key_terms.الْجَوَارِحِ: the limbs or bodily organs subject to injury rulings
key_terms.الْعَيْنَيْنِ: the two eyes, mentioned as analogous in legal ruling
key_terms.لِسَانَ: the tongue, as the injured bodily organ under legal consideration
key_terms.وَجَعٌ: pain or illness causing loss of function

ai.seo_question: What is the diyah ruling for cutting the tongue of a mute person in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on compensation for cutting the tongue of a mute person, distinguishing between one born mute and one who lost speech later due to illness or affliction. It also states that the same judicial principle applies to the eyes and limbs, and attributes this ruling to the Book of ʿAlī عليه السلام.
